quote: Indeed, in within-subject comparisons, a majority of subjects express both preferences simultaneously.
content: The high rates come from hypothetical questions put to student samples; the incentivized and representative-sample literature is much less impressive. Conlisk's "Three Variants on the Allais Example" (American Economic Review 79, 1989) showed that perturbing the certain option by a hair — replacing "$24,000 for sure" with a 99% chance — sharply reduces the violation rate, which means much of the effect is attached to the presentation of certainty rather than to a stable preference over lotteries. Huck and Müller's study of a large representative sample with real money ("Allais for all," Journal of Risk and Uncertainty 44, 2012) found the common-consequence effect only at high stakes and in some subgroups. That an effect exists is not in doubt; that a majority of people robustly hold this pattern when money is on the table is a stronger claim than the citations support.

quote: These two equations are algebraically inconsistent, regardless of U, so the Allais Paradox has nothing to do with the diminishing marginal utility of money.
content: This is correct and worth stating plainly, because it is the most common confusion about the example: readers reach for risk aversion, and risk aversion cannot produce this pattern, since the second pair is the first pair scaled by a common factor and any concave U cancels out of the comparison. The essay's construction of the pair is clean and the algebra is right. What follows from it is narrower than what the essay goes on to claim: the demonstration shows the pattern is inconsistent with expected-utility representation, which is the independence axiom's doing, not that it is inconsistent with having coherent values.

quote: All the axioms are consequences, as well as antecedents, of a consistent utility function.
content: This is true and empty: "consistent" here means "representable by an expected-utility function," so the sentence says the axioms are equivalent to the axioms. The von Neumann–Morgenstern result is a representation theorem — it tells you what an agent looks like if the axioms hold — and it cannot by itself establish that independence is a requirement of rationality any more than it establishes completeness, which almost no one defends as a rational requirement and which is equally load-bearing in the proof. Independence has been the disputed axiom since Allais put it to Savage in 1952, and Samuelson, Machina, and Quiggin all treated it as a substantive assumption about the separability of outcomes across mutually exclusive states. Calling its denial a departure from "the Bayesian Way" names the position rather than defending it.

quote: There is always a price for leaving the Bayesian Way. That’s what coherence and uniqueness theorems are all about.
content: The money pump built two paragraphs later extracts exactly two cents and then stops; it is not a pump. A genuine pump requires cyclic preferences that can be cycled indefinitely, and the Allais pattern is not cyclic — the agent's preferences over the lotteries are transitive and complete. What the construction exploits is myopia at the choice nodes, and the standard response since Machina's "Dynamic Consistency and Non-Expected Utility Models of Choice Under Uncertainty" (Journal of Economic Literature 27, 1989) is that a non-expected-utility agent who can see the tree coming plans over it, either by backward induction with consistent planning or by McClennen's resolute choice, and pays nothing. Gustafsson's book-length reconstruction of money-pump arguments (Money-Pump Arguments, Cambridge, 2022 — a book, no DOI) makes the auxiliary premises explicit; they are not free.

quote: How naive, how foolish, how simplistic is Bayesian decision theory…
content: The sarcasm is aimed at Maurice Allais, who was not making a naive point and who received the 1988 Nobel Memorial Prize in part for this line of work. His claim was that the independence axiom fails to respect complementarity between outcomes across states — that the value of a gamble can depend on its whole distribution and not only on state-by-state substitutions — and this claim was subsequently formalized into working theories. Rank-dependent expected utility (Quiggin, Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization 3, 1982) and cumulative prospect theory (Tversky and Kahneman 1992) give preferences that are complete, transitive, and monotone with respect to stochastic dominance, violating only independence. Those agents cannot be cycled, so the taxi-ride argument in the next essay does not reach them.

quote: the same failure to proportionally devalue the emotional impact of small probabilities is responsible for the lottery
content: Overweighting of small probabilities is a real and well-estimated feature of the probability weighting function, but it is not established as the cause of lottery play, and the two best-documented rivals cut against it. Lottery demand tracks the consumption value of anticipation and of having a ticket to imagine winning with, and it tracks skewness preference — buyers pay for the shape of the tail, not merely misperceive its probability. Both rivals predict the same purchasing behaviour, so the observation that people buy tickets does not discriminate among them. The parenthesis is a hypothesis presented as a conclusion, in an essay whose thesis is that intuitions about probability should not be trusted without checking.
